## The grid renders with zero width, or collapses to nothing

`GridLayoutComponent` measures its own root element's `offsetWidth`,
and only commits that value to `containerWidth` (and emits it on the
DI-scoped event bus other `GridItemComponent`s and the breakpoint logic
read from) `if (el.offsetWidth > 0 && el.offsetWidth !== this
.containerWidth)` — a guard against the well-known case where
`offsetWidth` reads `0` while an element (or one of its ancestors) has
`display: none`, is behind an `*ngIf` that hasn't resolved yet, or
hasn't been laid out by the time `ngAfterViewInit` runs. When that
guard fails, the grid doesn't error — it silently keeps whatever width
it last measured, which looks like a frozen or collapsed layout with no
console output to explain why.

Most common causes:

- Rendering `<kdl-grid-layout>` inside an `*ngIf`-gated
  tab/panel/modal that starts hidden — `*ngIf` fully removes the
  element (and its `ngAfterViewInit`/`ResizeObserver` setup) until the
  condition flips. Prefer `[hidden]` or a CSS visibility toggle for
  anything containing a grid, or trigger a manual re-measure right
  after the panel becomes visible.
- A flex/grid parent that hasn't completed its own layout pass on the
  same change-detection cycle the grid initializes in.
- The container has no defined height and depends on the grid's own
  content to size it, while the grid depends on the container for
  width — a sizing cycle that resolves to zero either way.

## Dragging doesn't start on some (or all) items

If a `GridItemComponent`'s `dragAllowFrom` `@Input()` is set, that
selector is checked **first, and exclusively** — a pointer-down target
that doesn't match it is rejected outright, and `dragIgnoreFrom` never
even gets evaluated. A `dragAllowFrom` selector that doesn't match
anything inside that item's projected content (a typo, or markup that
changed after the selector was written) silently disables dragging for
the whole item — there's no warning, since from the library's
perspective this is working as configured.

Check, in order:

1. Is `dragAllowFrom` set on this `GridItemComponent`? If so, does the
   selector actually match an element inside its `<ng-content>` right
   now?
2. Is `isDraggable` `false` on this specific `GridItemComponent`,
   overriding the grid-wide cascade?
3. Is the grid-wide `isDraggable` `@Input()` on `GridLayoutComponent`
   itself `false`?

Breakpoint resolution is driven by the grid **container's own measured
width** (the same value from the section above, propagated via the
DI-scoped event bus) — never `window.innerWidth`. This is deliberate
and correct for grids embedded in a sidebar, iframe, or any container
narrower than the viewport, but it means the zero-width failure mode
above has a second symptom: if the container never gets a real
measured width, breakpoint switching doesn't run either, since it's
derived from the same stuck value.

These come from the core validators (`layoutValidator`,

than debugging from the message alone:

- **`Layout can not be empty`** — an empty array was passed as the
  initial `layout` `@Input()`; render nothing (or a placeholder) until
  you have at least one item, rather than binding `[]`.
- **`Layout is not valid`** / **`Invalid parameter layoutItem id
  passed`** — every item needs a unique, stable `i`; duplicate or
  missing ids fail here.
- **`Invalid parameter cols passed`** / **`Parameter cols must be
  greater than 0`** — `colNum` (or a responsive breakpoint's own column
  count) resolved to `0` or `NaN`, usually because it's bound to a
  value that hasn't been set by the time the component initializes.
- **`Invalid parameter marginPx passed`** — `margin` expects a
  `[number, number]` pixel tuple, not a CSS string like `"8px"`.

```sh
npm i keystone-dashboard-layout-core
```

Works with `import`, `require`, and TypeScript's own type resolution —
the package ships ESM, CJS, and its own `.d.ts` types, so no extra

```ts
import { collides, compactLayout, getBreakpointFromWidth } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

## The cross-grid-registry subpath

Everything above comes from the package's own main entry point. One
piece is deliberately **not** re-exported there: the cross-grid
registry — the runtime coordination point multiple grids on the same
page use to recognize each other for drag-and-drop between them. It's
a stateful, singleton-style module tied to component mount/unmount,
not a pure calculation the way everything else here is, so it's kept
as its own, explicit subpath import instead of bundled into the main
one:

```ts
import { registerCrossGridZone } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core/gridlayout/helpers/cross-grid-registry';
import type { ICrossGridZone } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core/gridlayout/interfaces/cross-grid.interfaces';
```

Only worth reaching for directly if you're building a new framework
integration from scratch — the Vue and React packages already wire this
up internally for their own `allowCrossGridDrag` prop.

A config-to-Input()/Output() mapping for converting an existing angular-gridster2 integration to this library, verified against angular-gridster2's own current source.

This covers **`angular-gridster2`** — the most widely-adopted
Angular-specific option compared in
[Comparison: alternatives](/angular/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/).
The two libraries model a grid differently in a few real ways (not just
naming), covered in [Behavioral differences](#behavioral-differences)
below — read that section before assuming a straight rename covers
everything.

## Install

```sh
npm uninstall angular-gridster2
npm install keystone-dashboard-layout-angular
```

```diff
- import { GridsterComponent, GridsterItemComponent, GridsterConfig, GridsterItem } from 'angular-gridster2';
+ import { GridLayoutComponent, GridItemComponent } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-angular';
+ import type { TLayout, ILayoutItem } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

```diff
- <gridster [options]="options">
-   <gridster-item [item]="item" *ngFor="let item of dataset">{{ item.i }}</gridster-item>
- </gridster>
+ <kdl-grid-layout [layout]="layout" (layoutChange)="layout = $event">
+   @for (item of layout; track item.i) {
+     <kdl-grid-item [i]="item.i" [x]="item.x" [y]="item.y" [w]="item.w" [h]="item.h">{{ item.i }}</kdl-grid-item>
+   }
+ </kdl-grid-layout>
```

The most fundamental difference is right there: `angular-gridster2`
splits grid-wide config (`GridsterConfig`, passed as one `[options]`
object) from item data (`GridsterItem[]`, a separate array) — dragging
or resizing mutates items in place via callbacks. This library controls
everything through one `layout` array and one `(layoutChange)` output;
nothing is mutated in place. See
[Behavioral differences](#behavioral-differences) for what that changes
in practice.

## `GridsterConfig` → `GridLayoutComponent` `@Input()` mapping

Verified directly against `angular-gridster2`'s own
`GridsterConfig`/`Draggable`/`Resizable` type definitions.

| angular-gridster2 (`GridsterConfig`) | This library | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `maxRows` | `maxRows` | Same name. |
| `fixedRowHeight` | `rowHeight` | Same purpose. |
| `maxCols` | `colNum` | `angular-gridster2` also has `minCols`; this library has no minimum-column equivalent. |
| `margin` (single `number`, all sides) | `margin` (`[horizontal, vertical]` tuple) | **Different shape**, not just a rename — `angular-gridster2` applies one number uniformly; this library takes separate horizontal/vertical values. |
| `outerMargin`/`outerMarginTop`/`Right`/`Bottom`/`Left` | *(no equivalent)* | Apply padding on the grid's own container element in CSS instead. |
| `draggable.enabled` | `isDraggable` | Same. |
| `draggable.dragHandleClass` | `dragAllowFrom` | Same purpose — `angular-gridster2` takes a bare class name, this library takes a full CSS selector (so a class name still works, just written `.your-class`). |
| `resizable.enabled` | `isResizable` | Same. |
| `resizable.handles` (`{ s?, e?, n?, w?, se?, ne?, sw?, nw? }` object) | `resizeHandles` (`TResizeHandle[]` array) | Same 8 positions, different shape — an object of booleans there, an array of the enabled ones here. |
| `pushItems` | `preventCollision` (inverted) | `pushItems: true` (the `angular-gridster2` default) pushes colliding items aside — equivalent to this library's default, `preventCollision: false`. `pushItems: false` blocks the move entirely — equivalent to `preventCollision: true`. **The boolean is inverted**, not renamed. |
| `compactType` (14 string variants, e.g. `'compactUp&Left'`) | `compactType` (`ECompactType`, 5 variants) | Same name, **not the same enum** — see [Behavioral differences](#behavioral-differences). |
| `swap` | *(no equivalent)* | See [Behavioral differences](#behavioral-differences). |
| `displayGrid` (`'always' \| 'onDrag&Resize' \| 'none'`) | `showGridLines` (boolean) | This library has no `'onDrag&Resize'`-only mode — it's always-on or always-off. |
| `dirType` (`'ltr' \| 'rtl'`) | `isMirrored` (boolean) | Same purpose, boolean instead of a string enum. |
| `itemChangeCallback` / `itemResizeCallback` | `layoutChange` | Both `angular-gridster2` callbacks collapse into this library's single `(layoutChange)` output — it doesn't distinguish a move from a resize at the callback level. |
| `disableWindowResize` | *(no equivalent)* | This library always re-measures its own container via `ResizeObserver`; there's no flag to opt out of that. |

## `GridsterItem` → layout-entry field mapping

| angular-gridster2 (`GridsterItem`/`GridsterItemConfig`) | This library | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x`, `y` | `x`, `y` | Same. |
| **`rows`** | **`h`** | Renamed. |
| **`cols`** | **`w`** | Renamed. |
| `dragEnabled` | `isDraggable` | Same, per-item override. |
| `resizeEnabled` | `isResizable` | Same, per-item override. |
| `resizableHandles` | `resizeHandles` | Same 8-position/array-vs-object shape difference as the grid-wide version above. |
| `minItemRows` / `maxItemRows` | `minH` / `maxH` | Renamed. |
| `minItemCols` / `maxItemCols` | `minW` / `maxW` | Renamed. |
| `itemAspectRatio` (`number`) | `preserveAspectRatio` (`boolean`) | Different model — `angular-gridster2` takes an explicit target ratio; this library locks whatever the item's *current* `w`/`h` ratio happens to be. |
| `compactEnabled` | *(no per-item equivalent)* | Compaction here is a grid-wide `compactType`/`compactor`, not toggleable per item. |
| *(none)* | **`isStatic`** | This library's per-item "not draggable, not resizable, excluded from collision" flag has no single-field `angular-gridster2` equivalent — combine `dragEnabled: false` + `resizeEnabled: false` there for the closest match, though items still participate in `angular-gridster2`'s own collision cascade unless further configured. |

## Behavioral differences

- **Controlled-array model, not in-place mutation.** `angular-gridster2`
  mutates each `GridsterItem` in place (`x`/`y`/`rows`/`cols` change on
  the same object references you passed in) and tells you about it via
  `itemChangeCallback`/`itemResizeCallback`. This library's
  `GridLayoutComponent` is **fully controlled**: it never mutates
  `layout` — every change comes back as a brand-new array via
  `(layoutChange)`, the same pattern as a template-driven form control.
  Code that reads/writes item fields in place will need to switch to
  replacing the whole array on each `(layoutChange)`.
- **`compactType` shares a name but not a value set.**
  `angular-gridster2` has 14 directional compaction modes (up/left/
  right/down and diagonal combinations). This library has 5
  (`VERTICAL`, `HORIZONTAL`, `NONE`, `VERTICAL_OVERLAP`,
  `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`), plus a fully custom `compactor` for anything
  else — see [Pluggable compaction](https://kdla.winnem.tech/examples/42-pluggable-compaction).
  There is no direct mapping from most of `angular-gridster2`'s
  diagonal modes; `'compactUp'` → `ECompactType.VERTICAL` and
  `'none'` → `ECompactType.NONE` are the only clean 1:1s.
- **No swap-on-drag.** `angular-gridster2`'s `swap: true` lets dragging
  one item onto another of the same size trade positions instead of
  pushing. This library only pushes via compaction — an item landing on
  another never swaps with it (already noted as a gap in
  [Comparison: alternatives](/angular/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)).
- **`pushItems` is inverted, not renamed** (see the table above) — a
  literal find-and-replace of the option name will silently flip your
  collision behavior.
What keystone-dashboard-layout-core is, who it's for, and how it relates to the Vue/React/Angular packages.

`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` is the shared implementation
underneath every framework package in this project. Collision
detection, bin-packing, compaction, responsive breakpoint resolution,
alignment guides, and more all live here exactly once — the Vue, React,
and Angular packages each call into this same code rather than
maintaining their own copies of the hard, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong
parts of a drag-and-drop grid.

## Who this is for

Most people don't need this page at all — installing
**[Vue](/vue/)**, **[React](/react/)**, or **[Angular](/angular/)**
already pulls this in as a dependency, and none of its exports need to
be touched directly to use any of those three packages normally.

This package is worth installing and using **directly** when you want
the same algorithms *without* any of those three components — for
example:

- Validating a layout array (bounds, key uniqueness, margin/breakpoint
  shape) on a server, before it ever reaches a browser.
- Computing compaction or collision resolution for a batch job — a
  script that rearranges saved dashboard layouts in bulk, say — with no
  UI involved at all.
- Building an integration for a framework this project doesn't ship a
  package for (Svelte, Solid, a plain web component, or anything else)
  — the same drag/resize engine, breakpoint logic, and layout math the
  three existing packages use, without reimplementing any of it.

## What's genuinely framework-free, and what isn't

The large majority of this package's own exports are pure functions:
plain data in, plain data out, no live DOM or component lifecycle
required at all. That covers collision detection, bin-packing,
compaction (all five built-in strategies), pixel-to-grid-unit math,
alignment-guide/snap calculation, multi-select align/distribute/range
commands, responsive breakpoint resolution, layout serialization, SVG
export, and every validator.

One deliberate exception: `createNativeDraggable`, `createNativeResizable`,
and `createNativeAutoScroll` (the native, Pointer Events-based
drag/resize engine both the Vue and React packages share) need a real
DOM to do anything at all — they attach real event listeners to real
elements. They're framework-*agnostic* (no Vue or React-specific code
whatsoever) but not DOM-*free*, unlike everything else this package
exports.

Every function, type, and validator keystone-dashboard-layout-core exports, grouped by what it does.

Every export below comes from the package's own main entry point
(`import { ... } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core'`) unless noted
otherwise. Grouped by what each does, matching how the package's own
source organizes them internally.

## Layout data shapes

The core types every other function on this page takes or returns.

- **`ILayoutItem`** — a single grid item: `i` (id), `x`/`y` (grid-unit
  position), `w`/`h` (grid-unit size), plus the optional per-item
  constraints (`minW`/`maxW`/`minH`/`maxH`, `isStatic`, `isDraggable`,
  `isResizable`, and more).
- **`ILayoutItemRequired`** — the subset of `ILayoutItem`'s own keys
  that must always be present (`i`, `x`, `y`, `w`, `h`).
- **`TLayout`** — a plain array of `ILayoutItem`.
- **`TResponsiveLayout`** — a per-breakpoint map of `TLayout`, keyed by
  breakpoint name.
- **`TBreakpoint`** — one of the library's own breakpoint name strings
  (`xxs`/`xs`/`sm`/`md`/`lg`/`xl`/`xxl`).
- **`TBreakpoints`** — a `Record<TBreakpoint, number>` of pixel-width
  thresholds.
- **`IBreakpoints`** / **`IColumns`** — the shape `breakpoints`/`cols`
  props take: one column-count or breakpoint-width value per
  breakpoint name.

## Collision detection

- **`collides(item1, item2)`** — do these two layout items overlap?
- **`getFirstCollision(layout, item)`** — the first item in `layout`
  that `item` collides with, or `null`.
- **`getAllCollisions(layout, item)`** — every item `item` collides
  with.
- **`findFirstFitSlot(layout, cols, w, h)`** — the first open
  `{x, y}` position (scanning row by row) a `w`×`h` item can be placed
  at without colliding with anything already in `layout`. What backs
  dropping a new item onto a grid from outside it.

## Movement

- **`moveElement(...)`** — move a layout item to a new position,
  resolving any resulting collisions by pushing affected items out of
  the way.
- **`moveToCorrectPlace(...)`** — settle an item that's ended up out of
  bounds (typically after a `cols` change) back onto the grid.
- **`moveElementAwayFromCollision(...)`** — push one specific item away
  from a specific collision, the lower-level primitive `moveElement`
  itself is built from.

## Compaction, cloning, and pixel-position styles

- **`compactLayout(layout, verticalCompact, minPositions?)`** /
  **`compactItem(...)`** — the vertical compaction pass (and its
  single-item primitive): removes gaps by moving every non-static item
  up as far as it can go without colliding. `minPositions` backs
  `restoreOnDrag` — a floor each item won't compact tighter than.
- **`compactLayoutHorizontal(...)`** / **`compactItemHorizontal(...)`**
  — the same algorithm, transposed to the x axis (`ECompactType.HORIZONTAL`).
- **`compactLayoutOverlapVertical(...)`** /
  **`compactLayoutOverlapHorizontal(...)`** — the `_OVERLAP` compaction
  variants: every non-static item moves straight to `y: 0`/`x: 0`
  unconditionally, with **no** collision checking — items are allowed
  to end up overlapping as a result, by design.
- **`cloneLayoutItem(item)`** / **`cloneLayout(layout)`** — deep-clone
  via a JSON round-trip with a custom replacer/reviver pair, so
  `Infinity`/`-Infinity`/`NaN` (a legitimate, common value for
  `y`/`x`/`minH`/`minW`/etc — "place past everything else, let
  compaction settle it") survive the round-trip instead of silently
  becoming `null` (`JSON.stringify`'s own well-known limitation).
- **`getLayoutItem(layout, id)`** — find one item by id (string or
  number), or `undefined`.
- **`setTransform`** / **`setTransformRtl`** / **`setTopLeft`** /
  **`setTopRight`** — pixel position/size → inline CSS style object,
  in each of the four positioning modes the `heightMode`/RTL
  combinations need.
- **`getBottomYCoordinate(layout)`** — the lowest `y + h` across every
  item, i.e. how tall the grid needs to be to fit everything.

## Pluggable compaction

The same interface `GridLayout`'s own `compactor` prop takes.

- **`ICompactor`** / **`ICompactorContext`** — the interface a custom
  compaction strategy implements, and the context object it receives.
- **`verticalCompactor`** / **`horizontalCompactor`** /
  **`noCompactor`** / **`verticalOverlapCompactor`** /
  **`horizontalOverlapCompactor`** — the five built-in strategies,
  each matching one `ECompactType` value.
- **`getCompactor(compactType)`** — look up the built-in strategy for
  a given `ECompactType` value directly.
- **`ECompactType`** — the enum backing `compactType` (`VERTICAL`,
  `HORIZONTAL`, `NONE`, `VERTICAL_OVERLAP`, `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`).

## Grid-unit ↔ pixel math

- **`calcXY(top, left, ...)`** — pixel position → grid-unit `{x, y}`,
  capped to the grid's own bounds.
- **`calcColWidth(containerWidth, marginX, cols)`** — the pixel width
  of a single column, given the container width, horizontal margin,
  and column count.
- **`calcGridItemWH(gridUnits, colOrRowSize, marginPx)`** — grid units
  (width or height) → pixel size, accounting for the margins between
  cells.
- **`clamp(value, min, max)`** — a plain numeric clamp, used throughout
  the position/size math above.

## Pointer-event helpers

Behind `calcXY`/`calcPosition`/`calcWH` in both the Vue and React
packages' own drag/resize hooks — plain DOM event reads and arithmetic,
genuinely framework-agnostic.

- **`offsetXYFromParentOf(event)`** — a pointer event's `clientX`/`clientY`,
  converted to a position relative to the event target's own offset
  parent (falling back to `document.body` when there isn't one).
- **`createCoreData(lastX, lastY, x, y)`** — the delta between this
  tick's position and the previous one, handling the very first tick
  (`lastX`/`lastY` are `NaN`) by reporting a zero delta instead of
  `NaN`.
- **`IDraggableCoreData`** — the shape `createCoreData` returns.
- **`IPoint`** — a plain `{x, y}` pair.

## The native drag/resize/auto-scroll engine

The one genuinely DOM-dependent part of this package — see
[Introduction](/core/guide/introduction/) for why. Built on the plain
Pointer Events API, shared as-is by both the Vue and React packages.

- **`createNativeDraggable(el, getOptions, onEvent)`** — wires up
  pointer-driven dragging on `el`: activation-distance gating (so a
  plain click isn't misread as a drag), `allowFrom`/`ignoreFrom`
  selector filtering, and `dragstart`/`dragmove`/`dragend` callbacks.
- **`createNativeResizable(root, handles, getOptions, onEvent)`** —
  the resize equivalent: one native listener per resize-handle
  element, each reporting which `IInteractEdges` combination it
  represents.
- **`createNativeAutoScroll()`** — `start`/`update`/`stop`: scrolls
  the nearest scrollable ancestor of a dragged/resized element while
  the pointer sits near its edge, at a speed proportional to how close
  to the edge it is.
- **`RESIZE_EDGE_MAP`** — the 8 resize-handle identifiers
  (`TResizeHandle`, e.g. `'se'`), each mapped to its own
  `IInteractEdges` combination.
- **`TDragActivationDistance`** — the shape `dragActivationDistance`
  takes: a single number for every pointer type, or a per-type object
  (`{mouse, touch, pen}`).
- **`INativeDragEvent`** / **`INativeDraggableOptions`** /
  **`INativeResizeEvent`** / **`INativeResizableOptions`** /
  **`INativeAutoScroll`** — the supporting types for the three
  functions above.

## Ordering, partitioning, and bounds

- **`sortLayoutItemsByRowCol(layout)`** / **`sortLayoutItemsByColRow(layout)`**
  — sort a layout for vertical or horizontal compaction respectively
  (row-major vs. column-major).
- **`getAllStaticGridItems(layout)`** / **`getAllNonStaticGridItems(layout)`**
  — partition a layout by its `isStatic` flag.
- **`correctBounds(layout, bounds, distributeEvenly)`** — pull any
  out-of-bounds item back within `bounds.cols`, either flush to the
  right edge or redistributed evenly depending on `distributeEvenly`.

## Alignment guides and snapping

- **`findAlignmentGuides(...)`** — the horizontal/vertical guide lines
  to show while dragging an item near alignment with another.
- **`findSnapAdjustment(...)`** — the position delta that would snap
  the dragged item onto one of those guides.
- **`findSpacingIndicators(...)`** — the equal-spacing distance labels
  shown between aligned items.
- **`IAlignmentGuide`** / **`ISpacingIndicator`** — the shapes these
  return.

## Multi-select commands

Pure position-adjustment computation — each framework package's own
multi-select feature calls into these rather than maintaining three
separate implementations.

- **`computeAlignAdjustments(...)`** — the position deltas to align a
  set of selected items to one shared edge (`TAlignEdge`).
- **`computeDistributeAdjustments(...)`** — the position deltas to
  distribute selected items evenly along an axis (`TDistributeAxis`).
- **`computeRangeSelection(layout, anchorId, targetId)`** — the
  Shift-click range-selection helper: every item between `anchorId`
  and `targetId` in layout order, inclusive.

## Responsive breakpoints

- **`getBreakpointFromWidth(breakpoints, width)`** — which named
  breakpoint a container width currently falls into (the highest
  threshold strictly below `width`).
- **`getColsFromBreakpoint(breakpoint, cols)`** — the column count
  configured for a given breakpoint.
- **`sortBreakpoints(breakpoints)`** — breakpoint names sorted
  ascending by their own pixel-width value.
- **`findOrGenerateResponsiveLayout(...)`** — the per-breakpoint
  layout cache/generation logic: reuses a cached layout for a
  breakpoint if one exists, otherwise scales the current layout to fit
  the new column count.

## Serialization, SVG export, and outside-drop

- **`serializeLayout(layout)`** / **`deserializeLayout(raw)`** — the
  `localStorage`-persistence pair every framework package's own
  layout-storage helper/hook/service uses internally.
- **`exportLayoutAsSvg(layout, options?)`** — render a layout as a
  standalone SVG string (one rect + label per item), for exporting a
  static snapshot of a dashboard.
- **`IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions`** — `colNum`/`containerWidth`/`margin`/
  `rowHeight`/`itemFill`/`itemStroke`/`labelColor`/`backgroundColor`,
  each with a sensible default.
- **`readOutsideDropPayload(event)`** — parses the payload carried by
  a drag originating from outside any grid (the `outsideDropAccept`
  feature).

## Localizable ARIA strings

- **`DEFAULT_ARIA_LABELS`** — the built-in English defaults
  (`closeButton`, `itemRoleDescription`, `moveInstruction`,
  `resizeInstruction`).
- **`resolveAriaLabels(layoutLabels?, itemLabels?)`** — merges three
  layers (defaults ← grid-wide override ← per-item override), the
  same resolution every framework package's own `GridItem` uses
  internally for its ARIA attributes.
- **`IGridAriaLabels`** — the shape both label-override layers take.

## Validators

The same ones `GridLayout`/`GridItem` use internally for their own
prop validation — reachable standalone, e.g. to validate a layout that
came from an API response before ever handing it to a grid component.

- **`breakpointsValidator(breakpoints)`** — confirms all 7 required
  breakpoint keys are present.
- **`keysValidator(item)`** / **`validateLayoutItemRequiredKeys(item)`**
  — confirms a layout item has its required keys (`i`/`x`/`y`/`w`/`h`).
- **`layoutValidator(layout)`** — validates an entire layout array.
- **`marginValidator(margin)`** — validates the `margin` prop's own
  `[x, y]` tuple shape.

## Shared enums and types

- **`EMovingDirections`** / **`TMovingDirection`** — the direction
  values keyboard move/resize reports internally.
- **`ITransformStyle`** / **`ITopLeftStyle`** / **`ITopRightStyle`** —
  the inline-style shapes `setTransform`/`setTopLeft`/`setTopRight`
  return.
- **`ICalcXy`** / **`ICalcWh`** — the `{x, y}` / `{w, h}` shapes
  `calcXY`/`calcGridItemWH` return.
- **`IGridItemPosition`** — the full pixel position+size shape
  (`left`/`right`/`top`/`width`/`height`) drag/resize state tracks.
- **`IGridItemWidthHeight`** — a plain `{w, h}` pair.
- **`IInteractEdges`** — the `{top, right, bottom, left}` boolean
  combination identifying which edge(s) of an item are being resized.

What Keystone Dashboard Layout for React is, what you get, and where to go next.

Keystone Dashboard Layout for React is a React component library for building
draggable, resizable, responsive dashboard grids — the kind of UI you'd
use for a customizable analytics dashboard, a widget board, or any screen
where users rearrange content themselves.

It's a TypeScript-first library built on the exact same shared
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` algorithms and native, Pointer
Events-based drag/resize engine the Vue package uses — both frameworks
share one implementation of the hard, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong parts
(collision, compaction, responsive breakpoint math) rather than each
maintaining their own copy. React has reached full feature parity with
the Vue package.

## What you get

- **`GridLayout`** — the container. A **fully controlled** component: it
  never mutates the `layout` array (or any item in it) you pass in —
  every drag/resize tick (and the compaction that follows it) is
  reported via `onLayoutChange` with a brand-new array. This is the same
  `layout`/`onLayoutChange` contract `react-grid-layout` itself uses,
  the idiomatic React pattern here rather than Vue's own two-way
  `v-model:layout` binding.
- **`GridItem`** — a single draggable/resizable cell. It only needs an
  `i` matching one of `layout`'s own entries — position, size, and
  `isDraggable`/`isResizable`/`isStatic`/`minW`/`maxW`/`minH`/`maxH` all
  live directly on that layout item, not as separate props on this
  component.
- **An imperative handle via `ref`** — `compactNow()`, `rearrange()`,
  `duplicateItem(id)`, `undo()`/`redo()`, `selectItem()`/
  `clearSelection()`, `alignSelected(edge)`/`distributeSelected(axis)`,
  `exportLayoutAsSvg()`, `scrollToItem(id)`/`focusItem(id)`, and more —
  the React equivalent of Vue's own `defineExpose`'d template-ref
  methods, reached via `forwardRef`/`useImperativeHandle` instead.
- **`useLayoutStorage`** and **`useLayoutPresets`** — hooks wrapping
  layout persistence (serializing to/from `localStorage`) and named
  layout presets.

There's also a real, exported close-button component
(`GridItemCloseButton`) and drag-handle component (`GridItemDragHandle`)
— useful when you want those same building blocks rendered somewhere
other than `GridItem`'s own built-in rendering (e.g. inside a custom
header). Most consumers should reach for the simpler, built-in path
first though: a close button is a built-in, per-item opt-in
(`showCloseButton` + an `onItemClose` callback you handle yourself),
and any part of an item is a drag handle by default, restrictable via
`dragAllowFrom`/`dragIgnoreFrom`.

## How it fits together

```tsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { GridLayout, GridItem } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react';
import 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react/style.css';
import type { TLayout } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';

function Dashboard() {
  const [layout, setLayout] = useState<TLayout>([
    { i: 'a', x: 0, y: 0, w: 2, h: 2 },
    { i: 'b', x: 2, y: 0, w: 2, h: 2 },
  ]);

  return (
    <GridLayout layout={layout} onLayoutChange={setLayout}>
      <GridItem i="a">A</GridItem>
      <GridItem i="b">B</GridItem>
    </GridLayout>
  );
}
```

`layout` is a plain array of `{ i, x, y, w, h, ... }` objects — one per
`GridItem`. You own that array; `onLayoutChange` hands you a new one
every time the user drags or resizes something, and you decide what to
do with it (usually just `setLayout`). Everything else (collision
resolution, compaction, responsive breakpoint switching) happens
automatically based on the props you set.

## Design goals

A few decisions that shape how the library behaves, worth knowing up
front:

- **You own the data.** `layout` is a plain, serializable array you
  control — the library never mutates it in place, only ever hands you
  a new one via `onLayoutChange`.
- **Sensible defaults, explicit overrides.** Most behavior (draggable,
  resizable, bounded, etc.) can be set once on `GridLayout` and
  inherited by every item, or overridden per-item when needed.
- **Idiomatic React, not a literal Vue-to-React transliteration.**
  Vue's `provide`/`inject` eventBus becomes React Context, its
  composables become hooks, its named slots become render props
  (`header`, `renderResizeHandle`), and its two-way `v-model` binding
  becomes the standard controlled-component pattern — the same
  underlying behavior, expressed the way each framework actually works.

Both are exposed on the [imperative handle](/react/api/interfaces/imperative-handle/),
only meaningful with `multiSelect` on. `alignSelected` treats the
**first-selected item** (insertion order, not an arbitrary one) as the
anchor — it never moves; every other selected item aligns to its edge
or center. Needs at least 2 selected items to do anything.

`distributeSelected` needs at least 3 — the two outermost items (by
actual position, not selection order) stay exactly where they are, and
only what's "in between" spaces out evenly across the span those two
already define, the standard design-tool "distribute" behavior.

Both respect `preventCollision` when it's on — an adjustment that would
land an item on top of a *non-selected* item is skipped for that one
item; landing on another item that's *also* part of the same
align/distribute batch isn't treated as a collision at all, since
that's frequently the whole point of the command.
Fixes for the most common real failure modes when integrating GridLayout for React — grid stuck at zero width, dragging not starting, breakpoints not switching, and layout validation errors.

## The grid renders with zero width, or collapses to nothing

`GridLayout` measures its own root element's `offsetWidth` via a
`ResizeObserver`, and only commits that value to state `if
(el.offsetWidth > 0)` — a guard against the well-known case where
`offsetWidth` reads `0` while an element (or one of its ancestors) has
`display: none`, hasn't mounted into a sized parent yet, or is
conditionally unmounted. A separate `hasMeasuredWidth` flag exists
specifically so an actually-small container isn't confused with "never
measured yet" — but if the guard keeps failing, the grid silently
stays at its unmeasured seed width forever, with no console output to
explain why.

Most common causes:

- Rendering `GridLayout` behind `{condition && <GridLayout />}`, which
  unmounts and remounts it — every remount re-seeds the width from
  scratch. Prefer keeping it mounted and toggling visibility with CSS
  (e.g. a `hidden` class) if the parent panel is shown/hidden
  frequently.
- A flex/grid parent that hasn't completed its own layout pass on the
  same render the grid mounts. Give the grid's parent container an
  explicit width or `min-width` rather than relying on content-driven
  sizing.
- The container has no defined height and depends on the grid's own
  content to size it, while the grid depends on the container for
  width — a sizing cycle that resolves to zero either way.

## Dragging doesn't start on some (or all) items

If a `GridItem`'s underlying layout entry sets `dragAllowFrom`, that
selector is checked **first, and exclusively** — a pointer-down target
that doesn't match it is rejected outright, and `dragIgnoreFrom` never
even gets evaluated. A `dragAllowFrom` selector that doesn't match
anything inside that item's rendered content (a typo, or markup that
changed after the selector was written) silently disables dragging for
the whole item — there's no warning, since from the library's
perspective this is working as configured.

Check, in order:

1. Is `dragAllowFrom` set on this item's layout entry? If so, does the
   selector actually match an element rendered inside its children
   right now?
2. Is `isDraggable` `false` on this specific layout entry, overriding
   the grid-wide default?
3. Is the grid-wide `isDraggable` prop itself `false`?

Note that per-item flags like `isDraggable`, `isResizable`, `minW`/
`maxW`, and `dragAllowFrom`/`dragIgnoreFrom` live directly on each
entry in the `layout` array here — not as separate props passed to
`<GridItem>`, which only takes `i` and looks its own data up from that
array.

## Responsive breakpoints don't switch when I expect them to

Breakpoint resolution is driven by the grid **container's own measured
width** (the same `ResizeObserver`-sourced state from the section
above) — never `window.innerWidth`. This is deliberate and correct for
grids embedded in a sidebar, iframe, or any container narrower than the
viewport, but it means the zero-width failure mode above has a second
symptom: if the container never gets a real measured width, breakpoint
switching doesn't run either, since it's derived from the same stuck
value.

## Server-side rendering (Next.js / SSR)

The `GridLayout` component itself has no explicit SSR guard, but it
also doesn't need one: the `ResizeObserver` and pointer-event listeners
are only ever created inside a `useEffect`, which never runs during
server rendering under React's own contract. The pieces that *do*
carry explicit `typeof window !== 'undefined'` guards are the optional
layout-persistence and layout-preset hooks (`useLayoutStorage`,
`useLayoutPresets`) — safe to call during SSR, they simply no-op until
the client takes over.

## `Invalid parameter ...` / `Layout is not valid` errors

These come from the core validators (`layoutValidator`,
`keysValidator`, `marginValidator`, `breakpointsValidator`) rejecting
malformed input before it reaches the rendering/collision logic. The
message names the actual problem — a few worth knowing up front rather
than debugging from the message alone:

- **`Layout can not be empty`** — an empty array was passed as the
  initial `layout`; render nothing (or a placeholder) until you have at
  least one item, rather than passing `[]`.
- **`Layout is not valid`** / **`Invalid parameter layoutItem id
  passed`** — every item needs a unique, stable `i`; duplicate or
  missing ids fail here. A common trigger in React specifically is
  deriving `i` from array index instead of a stable id, which breaks
  the moment the array is reordered or filtered.
- **`Invalid parameter cols passed`** / **`Parameter cols must be
  greater than 0`** — `colNum` (or a responsive breakpoint's own column
  count) resolved to `0` or `NaN`, usually from a computed value that
  hasn't initialized yet.
- **`Invalid parameter marginPx passed`** — `margin` expects a `[x, y]`
  pixel tuple, not a CSS string like `"8px"`.

Where a newly-added item actually lands is entirely up to the
consumer — the library only places it wherever `x`/`y` say to, then
compacts around it. Appending with `x:0, y:0` (or `y: Infinity`,
placed at the very bottom instead) and letting compaction settle it is
the simplest convention, but it never *reuses a gap* left by a removed
item — a new item always lands in a fresh row even when there's
clearly room higher up.

This demo's own `addItem` does a real first-fit bin-pack instead, via
this package's own exported `findFirstFitSlot` (from
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core`): remove an item from the middle of
the grid, then add a new one, and it lands in the gap left behind. The
toggle demonstrates a second placement strategy — appending to the end
of the first row specifically, falling back to the general bin-pack
once that row is full.

The two strategies only produce a *visibly different* result once
there's an actual gap for them to disagree about — on a fresh, packed
layout, both fill the first row left-to-right and wrap to a new row
the same way, so toggling it on or off looks identical. To see the
difference: remove item `1` (opening a gap at `x:3`), leave the toggle
on, then add an item — it skips that gap and lands past the row's own
rightmost occupied edge instead, rather than filling it the way the
general bin-pack would.

import CustomDragPlaceholder from '../../../../components/examples-react/25-custom-drag-placeholder.tsx'; import CustomDragPlaceholderSource from '../../../../components/examples-react/25-custom-drag-placeholder.tsx?raw'; import ExampleTryIt from '../../../../components/harness/ExampleTryIt.astro'; `GridLayout`'s own `renderPlaceholder` prop — the React render-prop equivalent of Vue's own `#placeholder` scoped slot — renders fully custom content at the drop target during *any* drag or resize, in-grid or outside-drop, instead of the default plain, dashed-outline box. {isDragging && placeholder && ( drop at x:{placeholder.x} y:{placeholder.y} )}
)} ``` Positioning and sizing are still handled automatically — the returned content is placed inside an already-correctly-positioned wrapper; only what's shown *inside* that box is yours to customize. Leaving this prop unset renders the existing plain box, exactly as before this prop existed. If you want a visual indicator with a different visual language entirely — edge-alignment guide lines or labeled distance badges rather than a box at the drop target — see [`showAlignmentGuides`](/react/components/grid-layout/props/) and [`showSpacingGuides`](/react/components/grid-layout/props/) instead.

| Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `'auto'` (default when unset) | Grows/shrinks to fit content — same as the older `autoSize: true`. In the demo above, this deliberately overflows the dashed frame, since nothing here constrains it. |
| `'fixed'` | No explicit height applied at all — the consumer's own CSS decides. Same as `autoSize: false`. |
| `'scroll'` | Same as `'fixed'`, but also applies an inline `overflow-y: auto`, so content taller than whatever height your own CSS gives it scrolls internally instead of overflowing. |
| `'fit'` | Height locked to `100%` of the parent container, with the same `overflow-y: auto` as `'scroll'` — for a grid meant to fill a fixed-size panel exactly. |

`null` (the actual prop default) defers entirely to the older `autoSize`
boolean — set `heightMode` explicitly to opt into any of these, no
behavior change for existing consumers who only use `autoSize`.
onLayoutReady fires once, after every item's size has stabilized; onLayoutChange fires on every subsequent change.

`layout-updated` event (which fires on mount and after every
subsequent mutation), this package reports every change through the
same `onLayoutChange` callback used everywhere else — there's no
separate "mount" event to distinguish it from an ordinary update, since
`onLayoutChange` itself isn't called at all until something actually
changes.

```ts
gridRef.current.selectItem('a');           // adds 'a' to the selection
gridRef.current.toggleItemSelection('b');  // toggles 'b' in/out
gridRef.current.deselectItem('a');
gridRef.current.clearSelection();
gridRef.current.selectedItems;             // a snapshot, not reactive — see note below
```

## Multi-select

Off by default (`multiSelect: false`) — every prior behavior is
completely unaffected when this stays off. When on:

- **Click** an item — selects only it, replacing any prior selection.
- **Shift+click or Ctrl/Cmd+click** — adds/removes that item from the
  current selection additively.
- **Click empty grid background** — clears the selection entirely.

Dragging or resizing any *selected* item while more than one item is
selected moves/resizes every other selected item by the same delta —
also works from the keyboard (arrow keys/Shift+arrow on a focused,
selected item), not just mouse/touch drag.

A passenger that's static, or has `isDraggable`/`isResizable`
explicitly `false` on its own layout entry, never moves or resizes as
part of a group gesture. A passenger's own `minW`/`maxW`/`minH`/`maxH`
are also respected individually during group resize — see item "d" in
the demo above, which stops at its own `maxW` of 3 even while the
other, unconstrained items keep growing.

:::caution[Deliberately scoped, not fully collision-aware]
The delta is applied directly to every other selected item's position
or size — there's no per-passenger collision detection against
*non-selected* items during the gesture itself. Compaction (per
`compactType`) still runs normally once the gesture ends.
:::

:::note[selectedItems is a snapshot, not reactive state]
Unlike Vue's own template ref (whose `selectedItems` is genuinely
reactive), the imperative handle's `selectedItems` here is a plain
snapshot — reading it directly in JSX won't re-render when selection
changes. Use `onSelectionChanged` (as this example does) to mirror the
current selection into your own React state instead.
:::

## Custom resize-handle rendering (`renderResizeHandle` prop)

A render prop on `GridItem` — receives the edge identifier (`'n'`,
`'s'`, `'e'`, `'w'`, `'ne'`, `'nw'`, `'se'`, `'sw'`) as its argument,
letting you render different content per edge/corner. Renders inside
the same small hit-area `showResizeHandles`/`resizeHandleColor` already
use for the color/visibility toggle — both can be combined, or the
render prop used on its own for a fully custom icon instead of a plain
colored dot.
isMirrored flips the entire grid for right-to-left locales — anchor edges, resize direction, and drag math all reverse together.

import OutsideDropAcceptPayload from '../../../../components/examples-react/34-outside-drop-accept-payload.tsx';
import OutsideDropAcceptPayloadSource from '../../../../components/examples-react/34-outside-drop-accept-payload.tsx?raw';
import ExampleTryIt from '../../../../components/harness/ExampleTryIt.astro';

<ExampleTryIt code={OutsideDropAcceptPayloadSource} filename="outside-drop-accept-payload.tsx" lang="tsx" playground>
  <OutsideDropAcceptPayload client:visible />
</ExampleTryIt>

`readOutsideDropPayload<T>(dataTransfer, mimeType?)` reads and
JSON-parses a `DataTransfer` payload by MIME type — never throws; a
missing MIME type or malformed JSON both return `null` rather than
propagating a `SyntaxError`. `mimeType` defaults to `'text/plain'`,
matching `dataTransfer.setData`'s own default. Imported from
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core` directly — this package doesn't
re-export it through its own barrel.

:::note[Why this one starts inside a fixed-height frame]
`layout` starts empty, and `GridLayout`'s own `autoSize` (default
`true`) sizes the container to fit its content — with zero items, that
collapses to almost nothing, leaving no visible area to drop onto at
all. `heightMode="fit"` inside a `.drop-zone-frame` with a real CSS
`height` fixes this: the grid fills that frame regardless of how many
items it currently holds, so there's always a genuine drop target.
:::

:::caution[A real gotcha with native drag-and-drop]
`dataTransfer.getData()` only returns real values during the `drop`
event itself — during `dragenter`/`dragover` (when `outsideDropAccept`
is actually called) it always returns an empty string, regardless of
what the source set. This is a genuine, confirmed bug this example
had at first: `outsideDropAccept` tried to parse the full JSON payload
to check its `kind` field, which silently rejected every drag — real
widget or not — since the payload was never readable at that point.
The browser showed a "not a valid drop target" cursor and the drop
never fired.

The fix: only `dataTransfer.types` (the list of MIME types present,
not their values) is reliably readable during `dragenter`/`dragover`.
This example's drag source now sets a second, value-less MIME type
(`'application/x-widget'`) only on the real widget, and
`outsideDropAccept` checks `dataTransfer.types.includes('application/x-widget')`
instead of trying to read the actual payload. The full JSON payload is
still read via `readOutsideDropPayload` — just at `drop` time, in
`onOutsideDrop`, where `.getData()` genuinely works.
:::

See [Drag, drop from outside](/react/examples/outside-drag-drop/) for
`allowOutsideDrop` itself.

`snapThreshold` is how close, in grid units, a dragged item's edge needs
to be to another item's edge before it snaps — default `1`. Unlike
[alignment guides](/react/examples/alignment-guides/) (`showAlignmentGuides`,
purely visual), this actually changes where the item lands: once the

in the final committed position on drop.

entirely and is excluded from the drag-collision cascade (other items
compact around it as a fixed obstacle).

:::tip[Common use case: dashboard "anchors"]

`undo()`/`redo()`/`canUndo`/`canRedo` are all exposed on the
[imperative handle](/react/api/interfaces/imperative-handle/), the
same `ref`-based pattern as `compactNow()`/`scrollToItem()`. A snapshot
is captured at the *start* of a drag/resize and committed at its

directly in JSX won't re-render when it changes on its own. This
example forces a re-render (via a small tick counter) on every layout

CSS custom properties and class names for customizing the grid's appearance.

Unlike the Vue package (which bakes most of its own defaults into
compile-time SCSS variables, mostly not runtime-overridable), this
package's stylesheet uses real, runtime-overridable CSS custom
properties throughout, under a consistent `kdl-` prefix on every class
name — confirmed directly from `packages/react/src/styles/index.css`.

## CSS custom properties

All of these are genuinely overridable from your own stylesheet after
importing `keystone-dashboard-layout-react/style.css`:

| Property | Default | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| `--kdl-transition-duration` | `200ms` | `transitionDurationMs` prop |
| `--kdl-transition-timing` | `ease` | `transitionTimingFunction` prop |
| `--kdl-grid-line-column-size` | `1px` | Computed from `colNum`/margin when `showGridLines` is on |
| `--kdl-grid-line-row-size` | `1px` | Computed from `rowHeight`/margin when `showGridLines` is on |
| `--kdl-resize-handle-color` | `rgb(94 94 94 / 45%)` | `resizeHandleColor` prop |

```css
/* After importing 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react/style.css' */
.kdl-grid-layout {
  --kdl-resize-handle-color: #38bdf8;
}
```

## Key class names

The library only ever sets/removes these classes — it never applies
inline styles for anything covered here, so overriding the class is
enough; there's no competing inline style to fight.

| Class | Applied when |
|---|---|
| `.kdl-grid-layout` | Always, on the root element. |
| `.kdl-grid-layout--active-drag` | While any item in this grid has an active drag (raises this grid's own stacking context, relevant for `allowCrossGridDrag`). |
| `.kdl-grid-layout--grid-lines` | `showGridLines` is on. |
| `.kdl-grid-item` | Always, on each item's own root element. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--draggable` | The resolved `isDraggable` is `true` for this item. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--dragging` | This item has an active drag in progress. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--resizing` | This item has an active resize in progress. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--static` | This item's `isStatic` is `true`. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--selected` | This item is part of the current `multiSelect` selection. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--has-header` | The `header` prop was provided. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--rtl` | This item participates in `isMirrored` (RTL). |
| `.kdl-grid-item--show-resize-handles` | The resolved `showResizeHandles` is `true` for this item. |
| `.kdl-grid-item-header` / `.kdl-grid-item-body` | The two regions created when `header` is provided. |
| `.kdl-grid-item-close-button` | The built-in close button, when `showCloseButton` is on. |
| `.kdl-resize-hint--n` / `--s` / `--e` / `--w` / `--ne` / `--nw` / `--se` / `--sw` | The (always-present, invisible-by-default) hit zone for each resize edge/corner actually rendered — see `resizeHandles`. |

```css
/* After importing 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react/style.css' */
.kdl-grid-item.kdl-grid-item--static {
  background-color: #1e293b;
}
```

## Border radius

Unlike every class above, `borderRadiusPx` is applied as an **inline
style** (not a class), so it always wins over any CSS you write for it
— use the `borderRadiusPx`/`useBorderRadius` props themselves rather
than trying to override this one via CSS.
Selects the built-in compaction strategy GridLayout uses via its compactType prop.

Re-exported from the package's main entry point as a real (value)
export, so you can both type `compactType` and compare/construct
against these at runtime.

```ts
enum ECompactType {
  NONE = 'none',
  HORIZONTAL = 'horizontal',
  HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP = 'horizontal-overlap',
  VERTICAL = 'vertical',
  VERTICAL_OVERLAP = 'vertical-overlap',
}
```

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | No compaction at all — items stay exactly where placed, gaps included. Colliding items still get pushed down out of the way; this is distinct from `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` below — turning compaction off has never meant turning collision resolution off too. |
| `HORIZONTAL` | Items compact leftward, floating to the smallest available `x` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` | Horizontal compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `x: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions entirely — matching `react-grid-layout`'s own `allowOverlap` semantics applied to compaction specifically. Items may end up visually overlapping as a result. |
| `VERTICAL` (default) | Items compact upward, floating to the smallest available `y` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` | Vertical compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `y: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions. Same overlap semantics as `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`, applied to the vertical axis. |

Replaces an older, separate `verticalCompact: boolean` prop — a single
enum-valued prop is easier to extend (the two `*_OVERLAP` members add a
capability the boolean couldn't express at all) and easier to reason
about than a growing pile of independent booleans.

See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/api/interfaces/compactor/) for the
`compactor` prop that lets you replace the algorithm entirely instead
of picking one of these five, and [Pluggable compaction (compactType &
compactor)](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a live demo
switching between all five plus a custom compactor.
Every event GridLayout emits, as an enum.

Re-exported from the package's main entry point as a real (value)
export, so you can both type an event handler's parameter and compare
against these at runtime.

```ts
enum EGridLayoutEvent {
  BREAKPOINT_CHANGED = 'breakpoint-changed',
  CHANGED_DIRECTION = 'changed-direction',
  COLUMNS_CHANGED = 'columns-changed',
  CONTAINER_RESIZED = 'container-resized',
  DRAG_END = 'dragend',
  DRAG_MOVE = 'dragmove',
  DRAG_START = 'dragstart',
  CROSS_GRID_DROP_REJECTED = 'cross-grid-drop-rejected',
  CROSS_GRID_ITEM_DROPPED = 'cross-grid-item-dropped',
  ITEM_DROPPED_FROM_OUTSIDE = 'item-dropped-from-outside',
  LAYOUT_READY = 'layout-ready',
  LAYOUT_UPDATE = 'update:layout',
  LAYOUT_UPDATED = 'layout-updated',
  MOVE_BLOCKED_BY_COLLISION = 'move-blocked-by-collision',
  SELECTION_CHANGED = 'selection-changed',
}
```

See [GridLayout events](/vue/components/grid-layout/vue-events/) for the
full payload/timing reference for each.

:::caution[Declared but not currently emitted]
`CHANGED_DIRECTION` and `CONTAINER_RESIZED` exist on the enum for
backwards compatibility but aren't wired up anywhere in `GridLayout` —
don't rely on either firing. (`GridItem` has its own, functioning
`CONTAINER_RESIZED` event — see [`EGridItemEvent`](/vue/api/enums/grid-item-events/)
— this is a separate, unused one on the layout itself.)
:::

`LAYOUT_UPDATE`'s value (`'update:layout'`) is Vue's own `v-model`
naming convention — it's what makes `<GridLayout v-model:layout="layout">`
work without you needing to listen for it directly.
Every event GridItem emits, as an enum.

```ts
  DRAGGED = 'dragged',
  MOVE = 'item-move',
  MOVED = 'item-moved',
```

The interface backing localizable ARIA strings, plus the built-in English defaults exported alongside it.
The interface behind the compactor prop, its context object, and the five built-in strategies exported alongside it.

```ts
interface ICompactor {
  readonly type: string;
  compact(layout: TLayout, cols: number, context: ICompactorContext): TLayout;
}
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | A short, descriptive name for this strategy — informational only (e.g. for logging); never read by `GridLayout` itself. |
| `compact(layout, cols, context)` | Compacts a layout, **returning a new array** — must not mutate the input `layout` or any of its items in place. |

## `ICompactorContext`

```ts
interface ICompactorContext {
  compactType: ECompactType;
  minPositions?: Record<string | number, { x?: number; y?: number }>;
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `compactType` | Which built-in strategy currently applies — informational, read from `GridLayout`'s own `compactType` prop at the moment compaction runs. A custom compactor decides for itself whether/how to use this; nothing enforces it. |
| `minPositions` | Present only during a `restoreOnDrag`-gated compaction (drag end) — the pre-drag position each item shouldn't rise/shift any tighter than. Absent for every other trigger (resize end, add/remove, mount, breakpoint change, `compactNow()`/`rearrange()`), and for the two `*_OVERLAP` types. |

## The five built-in strategies

Exported individually, as a starting point for a custom compactor to
delegate back to for part of a layout (e.g. compact everything except
one pinned row) rather than reimplementing standard compaction from
scratch:

```ts
import {
  verticalCompactor,
  horizontalCompactor,
  noCompactor,
  verticalOverlapCompactor,
  horizontalOverlapCompactor,
  getCompactor,
} from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-vue';
```

| Export | Backs |
|---|---|
| `verticalCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` (the default) |
| `horizontalCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL` |
| `noCompactor` | `ECompactType.NONE` |
| `verticalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL_OVERLAP` |
| `horizontalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` |
| `getCompactor(compactType)` | Looks up the built-in `ICompactor` matching a given `ECompactType` — the same mapping `GridLayout` itself uses internally when the `compactor` prop isn't set. |

See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a
full working custom compactor, and [ECompactType](/vue/api/enums/compact-type/)
for what each built-in strategy actually does.
The typed payloads for GridLayout's cross-grid and outside-drop events.
The payload shape carried on GridLayout and GridItem's internal eventBus.
Types for values reachable through a GridLayout/GridItem instance ref via defineExpose.
serializeLayout/deserializeLayout, useLayoutStorage, and useLayoutPresets — the exported building blocks and composables behind saving and loading a layout.
One entry in a GridLayout's layout array — every field a layout item can carry.

One entry in a `GridLayout`'s `layout` array. The optional fields mirror
the corresponding `GridItem` props (`isDraggable`, `minH`, etc.) —
Vue's own `GridItem` takes most of these as direct component props
rather than reading them from the layout item, so setting one here is
mainly useful for configuring items from data instead of template props.

```ts
interface ILayoutItemRequired {
  i: string | number;
  h: number;
  w: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface ILayoutItem<TMeta = unknown> extends ILayoutItemRequired {
  // ...optional fields below
}
```

`ILayoutItemRequired` is exported separately too, in case you need to
type just the required fields on their own (a minimal seed object before
optional fields are added, say).

## Required fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | Unique identifier, matched against a `GridItem`'s `i` prop. Must be either a non-empty string or a finite number — never both at once, and never an empty string. String matching against a `GridItem`'s own `i` prop is case-insensitive (`'Widget-1'` matches `'widget-1'`); number matching is exact. |
| `h` | `number` | Height, in grid row units. |
| `w` | `number` | Width, in grid column units. |
| `x` | `number` | Horizontal position, in grid column units. |
| `y` | `number` | Vertical position, in grid row units. |

## Optional fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | Per-item drag override. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | Per-item resize override. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean` | Excludes this item from dragging, resizing, and collision cascades. |
| `maxH` / `maxW` / `minH` / `minW` | `number` | Per-item size constraints. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | CSS `z-index` override, winning over the static/dragging/resizing CSS-class defaults. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | Per-item override; `undefined` defers to the grid-wide default. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | Per-item override for native auto-scroll near a container edge during drag/resize. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | Per-item override for locking width/height ratio while resizing. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | Per-item override, merged over the grid-wide `ariaLabels` prop and the built-in English defaults. |
| `dragAllowFrom` / `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selectors restricting where a drag can/can't start. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector for elements that shouldn't start a resize. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | Minimum pointer movement, in pixels, before a pointerdown counts as a drag — one value for every pointer type, or distinct values per mouse/touch/pen. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | Per-item override for restricting dragging to within the container. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | Restricts which of the 8 resize-hint spans render/activate for this item. An empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize" value, distinct from `isResizable: false`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | Whether this item participates in the grid's own RTL mirroring. Default `true`. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | Per-item override for the master interactivity switch. |
| `borderRadiusPx` / `useBorderRadius` | `number` / `boolean` | Per-item border radius override. |
| `showResizeHandles` / `resizeHandleColor` | `boolean` / `string` | Per-item visible resize-handle override. |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | Re-runs this item's own size measurement whenever its rendered content changes size. No grid-wide equivalent. |
| `moved` | `boolean` | Set internally by compaction/collision helpers to short-circuit infinite loops — not meant to be set by consumers. |
| `data` | `TMeta` | Optional, consumer-defined payload — never read or written by the library itself. Round-trips through serialize/deserialize like any other field, as long as it's JSON-serializable. |

## `TMeta` — attaching typed data to a layout item

```ts
interface IWidgetConfig {
  chartType: 'bar' | 'line';
}

const layout = ref<TLayout<IWidgetConfig>>([
  { h: 2, i: '0', w: 2, x: 0, y: 0, data: { chartType: 'bar' } },
]);
```

Attach whatever payload an item needs directly on the layout item,
instead of maintaining a parallel array keyed by `i` to look it up
separately. Every existing usage of `ILayoutItem`/`TLayout` without a
type argument keeps working unchanged — the default (`unknown`) only
matters if you actually read `.data` and want it typed as something
more specific.

## `TLayoutItem`

Structurally identical to `ILayoutItem`. Both exist in the codebase;
prefer `ILayoutItem` for new code — `TLayoutItem` is kept for backwards
compatibility with existing type annotations.
exportLayoutAsSvg and readOutsideDropPayload — two standalone utility functions exported from the package root.

## `exportLayoutAsSvg`

```ts
function exportLayoutAsSvg(layout: TLayout, options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions): string;
```

```ts
interface IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions {
  colNum?: number;          // default: 12
  rowHeight?: number;       // default: 150
  margin?: [number, number]; // default: [10, 10]
  containerWidth?: number;  // default: 1200 — must be supplied explicitly; see note below
  itemFill?: string;        // default: '#eef2ff'
  itemStroke?: string;      // default: '#c7d2fe'
  labelColor?: string;      // default: '#3730a3'
  backgroundColor?: string | null; // default: null (transparent)
}
```

Renders a `TLayout` as a standalone SVG string, each item drawn as a
labeled rectangle from the layout data alone — not a snapshot of
whatever's actually rendered inside each `GridItem`. Good for a
structural thumbnail of the layout itself, not a substitute for a real
screenshot of custom slot content. Never throws: an empty layout
produces a valid, empty SVG.

`containerWidth` has to be passed explicitly, unlike `GridLayout`
itself, which measures its own container automatically — there's no
DOM element for this standalone function to measure. Pass the same
width your actual grid renders at for a matching result.

The returned string is a complete `<svg>...</svg>` document — usable
directly, downloaded as a `.svg` file via a `Blob`, or drawn onto a
`<canvas>` first if a raster PNG/JPEG is specifically needed. See
[Export layout as SVG](/vue/examples/svg-export/) for a full example.

## `readOutsideDropPayload`

```ts
function readOutsideDropPayload<T>(
  dataTransfer: DataTransfer | null | undefined,
  mimeType?: string, // default: 'text/plain'
): T | null;
```

Reads and JSON-parses a native `DataTransfer` payload by MIME type —
every consumer of `allowOutsideDrop`'s `item-dropped-from-outside`
event otherwise re-implements the same `dataTransfer.getData(mimeType)`/
`JSON.parse` parsing by hand. Never throws: a missing MIME type or
malformed JSON both return `null`. Performs no runtime shape validation
against `T` — that's the caller's own responsibility, since the payload
is whatever the consumer's own drag source chose to attach.

:::caution[A real gotcha with native drag-and-drop]
`dataTransfer.getData()` only returns real values during the `drop`
event itself — not `dragenter`/`dragover`.
:::

See [outsideDropAccept & readOutsideDropPayload](/vue/examples/outside-drop-accept-payload/)
for a full working example.
The internal event bus, from GridItem's own side.

The same shared event bus documented on
[GridLayout's eventbus events page](/vue/components/grid-layout/eventbus-events/) —
this page lists them from `GridItem`'s perspective: what it listens for,
and what it emits.

## Listens for (pushed down from GridLayout)

`changeDirection`, `compact`, `setBounded`, `setBorderRadiusPx`,
`setColNum`, `setDraggable`, `setEnableEditMode`, `setMargin`,
`setMaxRows`, `setResizable`, `setResizeHandles`, `setRowHeight`,
`setShowCloseButton`, `setTransformScale`, `setUseBorderRadius`,
`setUseCssTransforms`, `updateWidth` — each has a corresponding handler
registered on mount and deregistered on unmount.

The `setDraggable`/`setResizable`/`setBounded`/`setShowCloseButton`/
`setEnableEditMode`/`setUseBorderRadius`/`setBorderRadiusPx`/
`setResizeHandles` handlers only apply the pushed value when the item's
own matching prop is `null` — an explicit per-item prop always wins
over the cascade. `setUseCssTransforms` is the one exception: it applies
unconditionally, since there's no per-item override for it at all.

## Emits (reported up to GridLayout)

`dragEvent` and `resizeEvent`, both carrying an `IEventsData` payload —
emitted on every `dragstart`/`dragmove`/`dragend` (or
`resizestart`/`resizemove`/`resizeend`) tick. `itemClicked` (an
`IItemClickedData` payload) fires on a genuine click/tap, backing
`GridLayout`'s own `multiSelect` handling.

See [GridLayout's eventbus events](/vue/components/grid-layout/eventbus-events/)
for the full message table and payload shapes.
Every prop GridItem accepts, with defaults and links to live examples.

`h`, `i`, `w`, `x`, and `y` are required — everything else has a default.
Props that can defer to a `GridLayout` default (`isDraggable`,
`isResizable`, `isBounded`) accept `null` for exactly that purpose.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `h` | `number` (required) | — | Height, in grid row units. |
| `i` | `string \| number` (required) | — | Unique identifier, matching this item's entry in the parent's `layout` array. Must be either a non-empty string or a finite number — never both at once. String matching is case-insensitive (`'Widget-1'` matches `'widget-1'`); number matching is exact. |
| `w` | `number` (required) | — | Width, in grid column units. |
| `x` | `number` (required) | — | Starting horizontal position, in grid column units. |
| `y` | `number` (required) | — | Starting vertical position, in grid row units. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | `{}` | Per-item overrides for localizable UI/ARIA strings. See [Localizable ARIA strings](/vue/examples/aria-labels/). |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | `false` | Scrolls the item's nearest scrollable ancestor automatically when a drag or resize approaches its edge. See [autoScroll](/vue/examples/auto-scroll/). |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | `false` | Automatically re-runs `autoSize()`'s measurement whenever the default slot's content actually changes size. See [Per-item autoHeight](/vue/examples/per-item-auto-height/). |
| `borderRadiusPx` | `number \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `borderRadiusPx`, itself `10` by default) | Border radius, in pixels, applied when `useBorderRadius` is true. See [Border radius](/vue/examples/border-radius/). |

| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | `null` (fixed 3px for every pointer type) | Minimum pointer movement, in pixels, before a pointerdown is treated as a drag rather than a click — one value for every pointer type, or distinct values per `mouse`/`touch`/`pen`. A pointer type left unset in the object form falls back to the same 3px default, not `0`. |
| `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string` | `` `a, button` `` | CSS selector for elements that should *not* start a drag. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `enableEditMode`, itself `true` by default) | Master switch — when `false`, the item can't be dragged, resized, or closed regardless of other props. See [Edit mode toggle](/vue/examples/edit-mode-toggle/). |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | `null` | Restrict dragging to within the container. `null` defers to `GridLayout`'s `isBounded`. See [Bounded drag](/vue/examples/bounded-drag/). |
| `isDraggable` | `boolean \| null` | `null` | `null` defers to `GridLayout`'s `isDraggable`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean \| null` | `true` | Whether this item participates in the parent layout's RTL mirroring. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean \| null` | `null` | `null` defers to `GridLayout`'s `isResizable`. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean \| null` | `false` | Ignores `isDraggable`/`isResizable` entirely; excluded from collision cascades. See [Static items](/vue/examples/static-items/). |
| `maxH` | `number` | `Infinity` | Maximum height, in grid row units. See [Size constraints & aspect ratio](/vue/examples/size-constraints-aspect-ratio/). |
| `maxW` | `number` | `Infinity` | Maximum width, in grid column units. |
| `minH` | `number` | `1` | Minimum height, in grid row units. |
| `minW` | `number` | `1` | Minimum width, in grid column units. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | `false` | Locks the width/height ratio while resizing. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | `null` | CSS selector for elements that should *not* start a resize. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `resizeHandles`, itself all 8 by default) | Which of the 8 resize-hint spans actually render/activate for this item — restricts resizing to specific edges/corners instead of the all-or-nothing `showResizeHandles` toggle. An empty array (`[]`) is a deliberate, valid "no handle-driven resize for this item" value, distinct from `isResizable: false` (keyboard arrow-key resize still works with `[]`; it doesn't with `isResizable: false`). |
| `resizeHandleColor` | `string \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `resizeHandleColor`) | CSS color for the visible resize handle, when `showResizeHandles` is true. |
| `showResizeHandles` | `boolean \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `showResizeHandles`, itself `false` by default) | Renders a visible resize-handle affordance instead of only a cursor change on hover. See [Configurable resize-hint appearance](/vue/examples/resize-hint-appearance/). |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `showCloseButton`, itself `false` by default) | Shows the built-in close button. Ignored when `isStatic` is true. See [Show close button](/vue/examples/close-button/). |
| `useBorderRadius` | `boolean \| null` | `null` (inherits `GridLayout`'s own `useBorderRadius`, itself `false` by default) | Applies `borderRadiusPx` as a border radius. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | `null` (no override) | Explicit stacking-order override, applied as an inline `z-index` style. Without it, the item falls back to the library's own implicit handling (static items sit at `-1`, an actively resizing item briefly rises to `3`, everything else uses normal DOM-order stacking). An explicit value here always wins over both, regardless of the item's current static/resizing state — useful for pinning one panel permanently above every other, including while others are mid-resize. |

## Resize direction support

All four edges — top, right, bottom, left — and their diagonal corners
are resizable. Left/top-edge resizes move the item's position (`x`/`y`)
as well as its size, since growing from the left/top edge means the
opposite edge stays fixed. In RTL mode, this is mirrored correctly too —
dragging the right edge (rather than the left) is what moves the
anchor. See [Mirrored (RTL)](/vue/examples/mirrored-rtl/).

## Default slot Anything you render inside `` lands here — text, images, forms, a chart component, another Vue component entirely. `GridItem` doesn't style it. ```vue ``` The slot receives one scope prop: | Prop | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `style` | `Record` | The same computed position/size style `GridItem` applies to its own root element — rarely needed, but available if a child needs to match it exactly (e.g. an absolutely-positioned overlay). | ```vue
Matches the item's own computed size exactly
 ``` ## `#header` slot An optional, separate header region above the default slot's own content — only affects layout when actually provided; the no-header case renders identically to before this slot existed. ```vue {{ item.body }} ``` When used, `GridItem` switches to a vertical flex layout: the header shrinks to fit its own content, and the default slot's content (now wrapped in its own scrollable region) takes whatever space remains — content taller than the item's own fixed pixel height scrolls internally instead of pushing the item's real size (which the grid's own layout math depends on staying accurate). ## `#resize-handle` slot Custom content for each of the 8 resize handles (edges + corners) — a fully custom render (an icon, not just a color) rather than only a color/visibility toggle. Renders inside the same small hit-area `showResizeHandles`/`resizeHandleColor` already use; both mechanisms can be combined, or the slot used alone for a fully custom look.
