A grid-to-image export utility — nothing previously captured the rendered grid as a static image (a report, a thumbnail preview, a "share my dashboard…

A grid-to-image export utility — nothing previously captured the
rendered grid as a static image (a report, a thumbnail preview, a
"share my dashboard layout" feature). Deliberately built as a
dependency-free SVG generator directly from layout data, rather than
a `html2canvas`-style DOM-to-canvas wrapper: the latter would need a
new runtime dependency shipped in this library's own bundle (or left
for the consumer to add themselves, in which case this helper adds
little value over them calling it directly on the rendered grid's
root element), and — being a real DOM screenshot — would be more
faithful to arbitrary custom slot content (a chart, an image) than a
hand-built SVG can be. This trades that fidelity for zero bundle-size
cost and no rendering dependency: it draws each item as a labeled
rectangle from the layout data alone, not a snapshot of whatever's
actually rendered inside each `GridItem`. Good for a structural
thumbnail/overview of the layout itself; not a substitute for a real
screenshot of custom content.

See
[Export layout as SVG](https://github.com/gwinnem/vue-responsive-grid-layout/blob/main/vitepress-docs/examples/28-example.md).

This trades that fidelity for zero bundle-size cost and no rendering dependency: it draws each item as a labeled rectangle from the layout data alone, not a snapshot of whatever’s actually rendered inside each GridItem. Implement this interface to replace `GridLayout`'s own compaction
algorithm entirely, via the `compactor` prop. `null`/`undefined`
(the default) means "use the built-in logic exactly as before this
prop existed" — this is a purely additive override, not a
replacement for `compactType`, which keeps working unchanged whether
or not `compactor` is set.

Called after every drag end, resize end, item add/remove, on mount,
on a breakpoint/column-count change, and by `compactNow()`/
`rearrange()` on demand — the same trigger points the built-in
compaction already ran at.

## Example

```ts
const shelfCompactor: ICompactor = {
  type: 'shelf',
  compact(layout, cols) {
    // Custom placement logic — must return a new array, never
    // mutate `layout` or its items in place.
    return shelfPack(layout, cols);
  },
};
```

***

### autoHeight?

> `optional` **autoHeight?**: `boolean`

Automatically re-runs this item's own height/width measurement
whenever its own rendered content changes size (a chart rendering
taller with more data points, for instance) — independent of the
whole grid being `autoSize`d/`heightMode`'d. Backed by a
`ResizeObserver` on a dedicated wrapper `GridItem.tsx` renders
around its own `children` only when this is `true` (`height: auto`
so it can actually grow past the item's own current fixed height,
unlike the item's own root element). No grid-wide default — Vue's
own version has none either, only a per-item `GridItem` prop.
Default `false`.

***

> `optional` **autoScroll?**: `boolean`

container edge during this item's own drag/resize — `undefined`
defers to the grid-wide `autoScroll` default. Same "Vue has an
equivalent prop, not a layout-item field" note as `zIndex` above
applies here too (Vue's own `autoScroll` is a `GridItem` prop, not
read from the layout item).

fixed 3px threshold for every pointer type — unchanged from before

library's own Vue and React components are both built on, with zero
framework dependency for the vast majority of it (every function

Every export here is re-exported from every other file that already
imported it before this entry point existed — this file adds a new
*public* door into code that was already internally shared and
already framework-free, not new logic. See `docs/REFACTORING.md` for
the import-path audit that confirmed nothing in this dependency
graph reaches into `@/components`'s own Vue component code (every
import of a layout/breakpoint type goes directly to its defining
file, e.g. `@/components/Grid/layout-definition`, never through the
main barrel) — the thing that would otherwise silently pull the
entire component tree into what's supposed to be a framework-free
bundle.

One deliberate exception to the "no live browser needed" promise
above: `createNativeDraggable`/`createNativeResizable`/
`createNativeAutoScroll` (from `native-interaction.ts`) need a real
DOM to do anything at all — kept here rather than duplicated into
each framework package specifically because they're genuinely
framework-agnostic (built on the plain Pointer Events API, no
Vue/React-specific code whatsoever), so both packages share this one
implementation. Still excludes what's tied to a *component's own*
lifecycle rather than being reusable as-is: DOM measurement
(`DOM.ts`), and the cross-grid registry (a runtime coordination
singleton tied to component mount/unmount, not a pure calculation).

Native replacement for interact.js's `autoScroll: { enabled: true }` — scrolls the nearest scrollable ancestor of `el` while the pointer is near its edge…

Native replacement for interact.js's `autoScroll: { enabled: true }` —
scrolls the nearest scrollable ancestor of `el` while the pointer is
near its edge during a drag/resize, at a speed proportional to how
close to the edge the pointer is. Started on `dragstart`/`resizestart`,
fed the latest pointer position on every `dragmove`/`resizemove`, and
stopped on `dragend`/`resizeend` — a `requestAnimationFrame` loop, not
a one-shot check per pointer event, since the pointer can sit
stationary near an edge and scrolling should still continue.

The default close button rendered inside a `GridItem` when
`showCloseButton` resolves `true`. Also exported standalone from the
package's main entry point, in case you want to render the same button
somewhere else (a custom header, say) and wire it to the same removal
logic yourself.

```tsx
import { GridItemCloseButton } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react';

function removeItem(id: string | number): void {
  setLayout((layout) => layout.filter((item) => item.i !== id));
}

<GridItemCloseButton i={item.i} onRemoveGridItem={removeItem} />;
```

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | — | The id of the `GridItem` this button removes when clicked. Required — unlike Vue's own `CustomCloseButton`, which needs a `-1` sentinel default since Vue props can't enforce "must be provided," React's own type system already expresses that directly. |
| `onRemoveGridItem` | `(id: string \| number) => void` | — | Called with `i` when the button is clicked. |

## Why you'd use this instead of `showCloseButton`

`showCloseButton` is the right choice for the common case — the built-in
button, styled via the classes documented in [Styling](/react/components/styling/).
Reach for `GridItemCloseButton` directly when you want the exact same
click/removal behavior but need to place it somewhere `GridItem`'s own
internal rendering doesn't reach — inside a custom header, for instance.
Not used internally by `GridItem` itself, which renders its own,
separate built-in close button with a matching visual style — the same
relationship Angular's own `GridItemCloseButtonComponent` has to its
package's built-in close button.
A standalone drag-handle widget, not used internally by the library — pair it with GridItem's dragAllowFrom.

A small drag-handle widget, exported for placing inside a `GridItem`'s
children when you want dragging restricted to a single handle rather
than the whole item — pair it with a layout item's own `dragAllowFrom`
field so only this element starts a drag.

:::caution[The grab target is a small circle, not the visible button]
The rendered markup is a labeled `<button>` **plus a separate**, small
decorative circle element carrying the `kdl-draggable-handle` class,
rendered as a *sibling* of the button — confirmed directly from the
component's own source. `dragAllowFrom` matches that circle
specifically, not the button/text you actually see labeled. Clicking
the visible text does **not** start a drag; only the small circle does.
:::

Not used anywhere internally in this library — a standalone, opt-in
utility component, exported from the package's main entry point
alongside `GridItemCloseButton`.

```tsx
import { GridItemDragHandle } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-react';

<GridItem dragAllowFrom=".kdl-draggable-handle" h={item.h} i={item.i} w={item.w} x={item.x} y={item.y}>
  <GridItemDragHandle text="⠿" />
  Item content
</GridItem>;
```

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text` | `string` | `'x'` | Label rendered inside the handle's own button, matching Vue's `CustomDragElement` default exactly. |

## Pairing with `resizeIgnoreFrom`

If the handle sits near a corner, it can land inside the same
edge-proximity margin the resize engine already uses to detect a resize
gesture — meaning grabbing the handle could start a resize instead of
the drag `dragAllowFrom` was meant to restrict things to. Excluding the
handle from `resizeIgnoreFrom` as well is what actually stops the two
from fighting over the same gesture:

```tsx
<GridItem
  dragAllowFrom=".kdl-draggable-handle"
  resizeIgnoreFrom=".kdl-draggable-handle"
  ...
>
```
The exact close button GridItemComponent renders internally for showCloseButton — exported for standalone reuse.

The default close button rendered inside `GridItemComponent` when
`showCloseButton` is `true`. Also exported standalone from the
package's own public entry point, for a consumer who wants to render
the same button elsewhere (e.g. inside a custom header) and wire it to
their own removal logic manually.

```ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { GridItemCloseButtonComponent } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-angular';

@Component({
  standalone: true,
  imports: [GridItemCloseButtonComponent],
  template: `<kdl-custom-close-button [i]="item.i" (removeGridItem)="removeItem($event)" />`,
})
export class MyHeaderComponent {
  removeItem(id: string | number): void {
    this.layout = this.layout.filter((item) => item.i !== id);
  }
}
```

| Input | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | — | `@Input({ required: true })` — the id of the item this button removes when clicked. Angular has first-class support for a required input with no default at all, unlike Vue's own `-1` "no item" sentinel workaround (needed there only because Vue's `withDefaults` requires *some* default for every prop). |

| Output | Payload | When |

| `removeGridItem` | `string \| number` | The button was clicked. Emits `i`. Named distinctly from `GridItemComponent`'s own local `removeItem` output, since this component has no relationship to any specific parent item — it's a standalone utility a consumer wires up manually. |

Like the React package (and unlike Vue's own mostly compile-time SCSS
variables), this package's stylesheet uses real, runtime-overridable
CSS custom properties throughout, under a consistent `kdl-` prefix on
every class name — confirmed directly from `packages/angular/src/styles/index.scss`.
Import it once, wherever you import `GridLayoutComponent`/`GridItemComponent`
from:

```ts
import 'keystone-dashboard-layout-angular/style.css';
```

## CSS custom properties

All of these are genuinely overridable from your own stylesheet after
importing the file above:

| Property | Default | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| `--grid-transition-duration` | `200ms` | `transitionDurationMs` input |
| `--grid-transition-timing` | `ease` | `transitionTimingFunction` input |
| `--kdl-grid-line-column-size` | `1px` | Computed from `colNum`/margin when `showGridLines` is on |
| `--kdl-grid-line-row-size` | `1px` | Computed from `rowHeight`/margin when `showGridLines` is on |
| `--kdl-resize-handle-color` | `rgb(94 94 94 / 45%)` | `resizeHandleColor` input |

:::note[Two of these have no `kdl-` prefix — a real, confirmed naming difference from React]
`--grid-transition-duration`/`--grid-transition-timing` are set exactly
this way in `grid-layout.component.ts` (checked directly, not assumed
identical to React's own `--kdl-transition-duration`/`--kdl-transition-timing`).
Both packages otherwise use the same `kdl-` prefix everywhere else —
this is a genuine, existing inconsistency in the published package, not
a documentation typo.
:::

```css
/* After importing 'keystone-dashboard-layout-angular/style.css' */
kdl-grid-layout {
  --kdl-resize-handle-color: #38bdf8;
}
```

## Key class names

The library only ever sets/removes these classes — it never applies
inline styles for anything covered here, so overriding the class is
enough; there's no competing inline style to fight. Three real naming
differences from the React package, each confirmed directly against
this package's own component source rather than assumed identical:
the grid-lines toggle is `.kdl-grid-lines` (not React's
`.kdl-grid-layout--grid-lines`), the outside-drop placeholder is
`.kdl-grid-placeholder` (not React's `.kdl-grid-outside-drop-placeholder`),
and there's no separate `.kdl-grid-item--show-resize-handles` gating
class at all — `--kdl-resize-handle-color` being set to a real color
(rather than the `transparent` default) is what makes a resize handle
visible here, with no class toggle needed alongside it.

| Class | Applied when |
|---|---|
| `.kdl-grid-layout` | Always, on the root element. |
| `.kdl-grid-layout--active-drag` | While any item in this grid has an active drag (raises this grid's own stacking context, relevant for `allowCrossGridDrag`). |
| `.kdl-grid-lines` | `showGridLines` is on. |
| `.kdl-grid-item` | Always, on each item's own root element. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--draggable` | The resolved `isDraggable` is `true` for this item. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--dragging` | This item has an active drag in progress. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--resizing` | This item has an active resize in progress. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--static` | This item's `isStatic` is `true`. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--selected` | This item is part of the current `multiSelect` selection. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--has-header` | A `kdlGridItemHeader`-projected header is present — bound on `.kdl-grid-item-inner`, the item's own internal wrapper div, not the host element itself. |
| `.kdl-grid-item--rtl` | This item participates in `isMirrored` (RTL). |
| `.kdl-grid-item-header` / `.kdl-grid-item-body` | The two regions created when a header is projected. |
| `.kdl-grid-item-close-button` | The built-in close button, when `showCloseButton` is on. |
| `.kdl-grid-item-close-button-icon` | A separate, empty, `aria-hidden` span drawing the "×" glyph in pure CSS — React's own button holds an inline "×" character directly instead, needing no separate icon element. |
| `.kdl-resize-hint--n` / `--s` / `--e` / `--w` / `--ne` / `--nw` / `--se` / `--sw` | The (always-present, invisible-by-default) hit zone for each resize edge/corner. |
| `.kdl-grid-placeholder` | The live drop-position preview while a native HTML5 drag (or a cross-grid drag) is over the grid. |

```css
/* After importing 'keystone-dashboard-layout-angular/style.css' */
kdl-grid-item.kdl-grid-item--static {
  background-color: #1e293b;
}
```

## Border radius

Unlike every class above, `borderRadiusPx` is applied as an **inline
style** (not a class), matching React's own approach — use the
`borderRadiusPx` input itself rather than trying to override this one
via CSS.
The interface behind the compactor input, its context object, and the five built-in strategies exported alongside it.

```ts
interface ICompactor {
  readonly type: string;
  compact(layout: TLayout, cols: number, context: ICompactorContext): TLayout;
}
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | A short, descriptive name for this strategy — informational only (e.g. for logging); never read by `GridLayoutComponent` itself. |
| `compact(layout, cols, context)` | Compacts a layout, **returning a new array** — must not mutate the input `layout` or any of its items in place. |

## `ICompactorContext`

```ts
interface ICompactorContext {
  compactType: ECompactType;
  minPositions?: Record<string | number, { x?: number; y?: number }>;
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `compactType` | Which built-in strategy currently applies — informational, read from `GridLayoutComponent`'s own `compactType` input at the moment compaction runs. A custom compactor decides for itself whether/how to use this; nothing enforces it. |
| `minPositions` | Present only during a `restoreOnDrag`-gated compaction (drag end) — the pre-drag position each item shouldn't rise/shift any tighter than. Absent for every other trigger (resize end, add/remove, mount, breakpoint change, `compactNow()`/`rearrange()`), and for the two `*_OVERLAP` types. |

## The five built-in strategies

Exported individually, as a starting point for a custom compactor to
delegate back to for part of a layout (e.g. compact everything except
one pinned row) rather than reimplementing standard compaction from
scratch. `ICompactor` itself and all five strategies below live in
`keystone-dashboard-layout-core`, not this package's own barrel:

```ts
import {
  verticalCompactor,
  horizontalCompactor,
  noCompactor,
  verticalOverlapCompactor,
  horizontalOverlapCompactor,
  getCompactor,
} from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

| Export | Backs |
|---|---|
| `verticalCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` (the default) |
| `horizontalCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL` |
| `noCompactor` | `ECompactType.NONE` |
| `verticalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL_OVERLAP` |
| `horizontalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` |
| `getCompactor(compactType)` | Looks up the built-in `ICompactor` matching a given `ECompactType` — the same mapping `GridLayoutComponent` itself uses internally when the `compactor` input isn't set. |

See [Pluggable compaction](https://kdla.winnem.tech/examples/42-pluggable-compaction)
for a full working custom compactor, and [ECompactType](/angular/api/enums/compact-type/)
for what each built-in strategy actually does.
One entry in a GridLayoutComponent's layout array — every field a layout item can carry.

One entry in a `GridLayoutComponent`'s `layout` array. The optional
fields mirror the corresponding `GridItemComponent` inputs (`isDraggable`,
`minH`, etc.) — Angular's own `GridItemComponent` takes most of these
as direct component inputs rather than reading them from the layout
item (the same shape Vue's `GridItem` uses), so setting one here is
mainly useful for configuring items from data instead of template
bindings.

```ts
interface ILayoutItemRequired {
  i: string | number;
  h: number;
  w: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface ILayoutItem<TMeta = unknown> extends ILayoutItemRequired {
  // ...optional fields below
}
```

`ILayoutItemRequired` is exported separately too, in case you need to
type just the required fields on their own (a minimal seed object before
optional fields are added, say).

## Required fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | Unique identifier, matched against a `GridItemComponent`'s `i` input. Must be either a non-empty string or a finite number — never both at once, and never an empty string. String matching against a `GridItemComponent`'s own `i` input is case-insensitive (`'Widget-1'` matches `'widget-1'`); number matching is exact. |
| `h` | `number` | Height, in grid row units. |
| `w` | `number` | Width, in grid column units. |
| `x` | `number` | Horizontal position, in grid column units. |
| `y` | `number` | Vertical position, in grid row units. |

## Optional fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | Per-item drag override. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | Per-item resize override. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean` | Excludes this item from dragging, resizing, and collision cascades. |
| `maxH` / `maxW` / `minH` / `minW` | `number` | Per-item size constraints. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | CSS `z-index` override, winning over the static/dragging/resizing CSS-class defaults. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | Per-item override; `undefined` defers to the grid-wide default. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | Per-item override for native auto-scroll near a container edge during drag/resize. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | Per-item override for locking width/height ratio while resizing. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | Per-item override, merged over the grid-wide `ariaLabels` input and the built-in English defaults. |
| `dragAllowFrom` / `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selectors restricting where a drag can/can't start. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector for elements that shouldn't start a resize. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | Minimum pointer movement, in pixels, before a pointerdown counts as a drag — one value for every pointer type, or distinct values per mouse/touch/pen. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | Per-item override for restricting dragging to within the container. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | Restricts which of the 8 resize-hint spans render/activate for this item. An empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize" value, distinct from `isResizable: false`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | Whether this item participates in the grid's own RTL mirroring. Default `true`. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | Per-item override for the master interactivity switch. |
| `borderRadiusPx` / `useBorderRadius` | `number` / `boolean` | Per-item border radius override. |
| `showResizeHandles` / `resizeHandleColor` | `boolean` / `string` | Per-item visible resize-handle override. |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | Re-runs this item's own size measurement whenever its rendered content changes size. No grid-wide equivalent. |
| `moved` | `boolean` | Set internally by compaction/collision helpers to short-circuit infinite loops — not meant to be set by consumers. |
| `data` | `TMeta` | Optional, consumer-defined payload — never read or written by the library itself. Round-trips through serialize/deserialize like any other field, as long as it's JSON-serializable. |

## `TMeta` — attaching typed data to a layout item

```ts
interface IWidgetConfig {
  chartType: 'bar' | 'line';
}

layout: TLayout<IWidgetConfig> = [
  { h: 2, i: '0', w: 2, x: 0, y: 0, data: { chartType: 'bar' } },
];
```

Attach whatever payload an item needs directly on the layout item,
instead of maintaining a parallel array keyed by `i` to look it up
separately. Every existing usage of `ILayoutItem`/`TLayout` without a
type argument keeps working unchanged — the default (`unknown`) only
matters if you actually read `.data` and want it typed as something
more specific.

## `TLayoutItem`

Structurally identical to `ILayoutItem`. Both exist in the codebase;
prefer `ILayoutItem` for new code — `TLayoutItem` is kept for backwards
compatibility with existing type annotations.

See [GridItemComponent props](/angular/components/grid-item/props/) for
the full table of these fields alongside `GridItemComponent`'s own
inputs.

## `exportLayoutAsSvg`

```ts
function exportLayoutAsSvg(layout: TLayout, options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions): string;
```

```ts
interface IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions {
  colNum?: number;          // default: 12
  rowHeight?: number;       // default: 150
  margin?: [number, number]; // default: [10, 10]
  containerWidth?: number;  // default: 1200 — must be supplied explicitly; see note below
  itemFill?: string;        // default: '#eef2ff'
  itemStroke?: string;      // default: '#c7d2fe'
  labelColor?: string;      // default: '#3730a3'
  backgroundColor?: string | null; // default: null (transparent)
}
```

Renders a `TLayout` as a standalone SVG string, each item drawn as a
labeled rectangle from the layout data alone — not a snapshot of
whatever's actually rendered inside each `GridItemComponent`. Good for
a structural thumbnail of the layout itself, not a substitute for a
real screenshot of custom projected content. Never throws: an empty
layout produces a valid, empty SVG.

`containerWidth` has to be passed explicitly, unlike `GridLayoutComponent`
itself, which measures its own container automatically — there's no DOM
element for this standalone function to measure. Pass the same width
your actual grid renders at for a matching result.

The returned string is a complete `<svg>...</svg>` document — usable
directly, downloaded as a `.svg` file via a `Blob`, or drawn onto a
`<canvas>` first if a raster PNG/JPEG is specifically needed. See
[Export layout as SVG](https://kdla.winnem.tech/examples/28-svg-export)
for a full example.

Not re-exported from this package's own barrel — import it directly
from `keystone-dashboard-layout-core` instead, same as the Vue and
React ports:

```ts
import { exportLayoutAsSvg } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

## `readOutsideDropPayload`

```ts
function readOutsideDropPayload<T>(
  dataTransfer: DataTransfer | null | undefined,
  mimeType?: string, // default: 'text/plain'
): T | null;
```

Reads and JSON-parses a native `DataTransfer` payload by MIME type —
every consumer of `allowOutsideDrop`'s outside-drop event otherwise
re-implements the same `dataTransfer.getData(mimeType)`/`JSON.parse`
parsing by hand. Never throws: a missing MIME type or malformed JSON
both return `null`. Performs no runtime shape validation against `T` —
that's the caller's own responsibility, since the payload is whatever
the consumer's own drag source chose to attach.

:::caution[A real gotcha with native drag-and-drop]
`dataTransfer.getData()` only returns real values during the `drop`
event itself — not `dragenter`/`dragover`.
:::

Same as `exportLayoutAsSvg` above, this isn't re-exported from this
package's own barrel either:

```ts
import { readOutsideDropPayload } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

See [outsideDropAccept & readOutsideDropPayload](https://kdla.winnem.tech/examples/34-outside-drop-accept-payload)
for a full working example.
Selects the built-in compaction strategy GridLayoutComponent uses via its compactType input.

Lives in `keystone-dashboard-layout-core`, not this package's own
barrel — a real (value) export there, so you can both type
`compactType` and compare/construct against these at runtime:

```ts
import { ECompactType } from 'keystone-dashboard-layout-core';
```

```ts
enum ECompactType {
  NONE = 'none',
  HORIZONTAL = 'horizontal',
  HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP = 'horizontal-overlap',
  VERTICAL = 'vertical',
  VERTICAL_OVERLAP = 'vertical-overlap',
}
```

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | No compaction at all — items stay exactly where placed, gaps included. Colliding items still get pushed down out of the way; this is distinct from `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` below — turning compaction off has never meant turning collision resolution off too. |
| `HORIZONTAL` | Items compact leftward, floating to the smallest available `x` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` | Horizontal compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `x: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions entirely — matching `react-grid-layout`'s own `allowOverlap` semantics applied to compaction specifically. Items may end up visually overlapping as a result. |
| `VERTICAL` (default) | Items compact upward, floating to the smallest available `y` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` | Vertical compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `y: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions. Same overlap semantics as `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`, applied to the vertical axis. |

Replaces an older, separate `verticalCompact: boolean` prop — a single
enum-valued prop is easier to extend (the two `*_OVERLAP` members add a
capability the boolean couldn't express at all) and easier to reason
about than a growing pile of independent booleans.

See [Pluggable compaction](/angular/api/interfaces/compactor/) for the
`compactor` input that lets you replace the algorithm entirely instead
of picking one of these five, and [Pluggable compaction](https://kdla.winnem.tech/examples/42-pluggable-compaction)
for a live demo switching between all five plus a custom compactor.
